problems.title: Load violations.csv with only three columns
problems.notebook: acc525/Data Analysis/Data Analysis (Part 1) - CLASS EXERCISE SOLUTIONS.ipynb
problems.prompt:
The course dataset `violations.csv` is in the working directory (68,841 rows, 11 columns).

Read it into a DataFrame called `data`, keeping only the columns `company`, `penalty` and `date` **by name**, then print `data.shape`.
hints: `pd.read_csv("violations.csv", usecols=[...])` keeps just the columns you list.
problems.solution:
import pandas as pd

data = pd.read_csv("violations.csv", usecols=["company", "penalty", "date"])
print(data.shape)
problems.tests:
assert list(data.columns) == ["company", "penalty", "date"], f"wrong columns: {list(data.columns)}"
assert len(data) == 68841, f"expected every row, got {len(data)}"
problems.test_summary: Checks the three columns and that all 68,841 rows were kept.

problems.title: How many violations involve Microsoft?
problems.notebook: acc525/Data Analysis/Data Analysis (Part 1) - CLASS EXERCISE SOLUTIONS.ipynb
problems.prompt:
Load `violations.csv` into `data` as the notebook does (`parse_dates=['date']`, `dtype={'gvkey': str, 'zip': str}`).

Filter the rows where `company` is `'Microsoft'` into a DataFrame called `microsoft`, then print `len(microsoft)` — a single number.
hints: A boolean mask like `data.company == 'Microsoft'` selects the rows.
`len()` of that DataFrame is the row count.
problems.solution:
import pandas as pd

data = pd.read_csv("violations.csv", parse_dates=["date"], dtype={"gvkey": str, "zip": str})
microsoft = data[data.company == "Microsoft"]
print(len(microsoft))
problems.tests:
assert isinstance(microsoft, pd.DataFrame), "microsoft must be a DataFrame"
assert len(data) == 68841
problems.test_summary: Checks the filter produces a DataFrame and the whole file was loaded.

problems.title: Publicly traded firms in December
problems.notebook: acc525/Data Analysis/Data Analysis (Part 1) - CLASS EXERCISE SOLUTIONS.ipynb
problems.prompt:
Load `violations.csv` into `data`.

Build `public12`: the rows whose `ownership structure` is `'publicly traded'` **and** whose `date` falls in December. Print `len(public12)`.

Two conditions on one DataFrame need parentheses around each one, joined with `&`.
hints: `data.date.dt.month == 12` only works once `date` is a datetime — read it with `parse_dates=['date']`.
Combine masks with `&`, and wrap each in parentheses: `data[(a) & (b)]`.
problems.solution:
import pandas as pd

data = pd.read_csv("violations.csv", parse_dates=["date"], dtype={"zip": str})
public12 = data[(data["ownership structure"] == "publicly traded") & (data.date.dt.month == 12)]
print(len(public12))
problems.tests: assert len(public12) == 3027, f"expected 3,027 publicly traded December rows, got {len(public12)}"
problems.test_summary: Checks the two-condition filter returns 3,027 rows.

problems.title: Count the missing zip codes
problems.notebook: acc525/Data Analysis/Data Analysis (Part 1) - CLASS EXERCISE SOLUTIONS.ipynb
problems.prompt:
Load `violations.csv` into `data` (read `zip` as a string so the leading zeros survive).

Print `data['zip'].isna().sum()` — the number of rows with **no** zip code — and remember the file has 68,841 rows.
hints: `dtype={'zip': str}` keeps zip codes as text.
problems.solution:
import pandas as pd

data = pd.read_csv("violations.csv", dtype={"zip": str})
print(data["zip"].isna().sum())
problems.tests: assert int(data["zip"].isna().sum()) == 68841 - 25337, "25,337 rows do have a zip code"
problems.test_summary: Checks the missing-zip count against the documented 25,337 non-missing values.

problems.title: Build a DataFrame by hand
problems.notebook: acc525/Data Analysis/Data Analysis (Part 1) - CLASS EXERCISE SOLUTIONS.ipynb
problems.prompt: A DataFrame is a dictionary of columns. Fill in the two blanks so the frame has a `company` column with two names and a `penalty` column with two amounts, sorted by penalty from high to low.
problems.starter_code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"company": ["Acme", "Globex"], "penalty": [5000, 25000]})
df = df.___(by="penalty", ascending=___)

print(df.iloc[0]["company"])

blanks.hint: The DataFrame method that sorts rows by a column.
You want the largest penalty first, so ascending has to be False.

problems.solution:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"company": ["Acme", "Globex"], "penalty": [5000, 25000]})
df = df.sort_values(by="penalty", ascending=False)

print(df.iloc[0]["company"])
